A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Medicinal plant-based hydrogel Microencapsulation

Ammonia decontamination in aquaponics

A B S T R A C T

The study investigates the use of microencapsulated product of Indian gooseberry (_Phyllanthus emblica_) devel-oped using hydrogel derived from isabgol (_Plantago ovata_) for ammonia removal in aquaponics water and the growth performance of _Pangasianodon hypophthalmus_ for a 45-day period. The study consists of a control (C) and two treatments: T1 (isabgol) and T2 (isabgol+Indian gooseberry). Ammonia was spiked weekly at varying concentrations. T2 showed significantly highest (_p_ < 0.05) ammonia removal in all the different spiking dosages,

followed by T1. Ammonia was eliminated more rapidly in the 4th week. T2 removed 83.24 ± 0.37 % of ammonia

in 36 h and 95.27 ± 0.59 % in 48 h. The decline in pH levels brought on by the nitrification process is connected with less ammonia removal in the 5th week. The fish growth indices (final total biomass, net weight gain, specific growth rate) and feed conversion ratio were significantly (_p_ < 0.05) improved in treatment groups, with T2

exhibiting superior performance. The hematological and serum biochemical analyses indicated reduced stress in

treatment groups compared to the control. The characterization of isabgol and gooseberry also revealed their potential as bioactive carriers. LC-MS analysis confirmed the presence of oxy-chromen-4-one, 4-indolecarbalde-hyde, kaempferol, and apigenin in isabgol. Phenolic acid, flavonoids, essential amino acids, and vitamins were found in Indian gooseberry. The study revealed that the developed product has the potential to decontaminate high ammonia levels, mitigate stress, and improve the growth performance of _P hypophthalmus_, which can be attributed to the controlled release and immunostimulating effect of microencapsulated Indian gooseberry product coupled with semi-biofloc formation facilitated by hydrogel derived from isabgol.

# Introduction

One of the food production sectors with the highest rate of expansion is aquaculture, which is essential to supplying humans’ daily demands for protein in their diets ([FAO, 2020](#_bookmark50); [Tacon, 2020](#_bookmark108)). Thus, it is believed that the most sensible aquaculture method is intensive fish farming, which relies on raising specific fish species in the accessible water ([Badiola et al., 2018](#_bookmark28); [Dawood, 2021](#_bookmark42)). However, intensive aquaculture effluent is largely contaminated with chemicals and bacteria that cause the fish to be stressed and hypersensitive. Excrement, metabolic byproducts, residual biocides and biostats, and uneaten feed waste are

the primary sources of these contaminants. It results in a decrease in dissolved oxygen and an increase in the sedimentation of organic ma-terial on pond bottoms ([Sriyasak et al., 2015](#_bookmark107)). At the same time, vari-ations in temperature and water acidity (pH) alter the ratio of unionised ammonia (NH3) that is generated, which can have detrimental effects on aquatic life and the ecosystem due to its toxicity ([Mook et al., 2012](#_bookmark85); [Mirghaed et al., 2019](#_bookmark84); [Yousefi et al., 2020](#_bookmark119)). In addition to inducing oxidative stress and immunosuppression ([Zhang et al., 2020](#_bookmark122)), ammonia poisoning results in growth retardation, metabolism disorder, increased susceptibility to illness, gill damage, and other physiological abnor-malities ([Ip and Chew, 2010](#_bookmark62); [Li et al., 2016](#_bookmark76); [Qi et al., 2017](#_bookmark92); [Parvathy](#_bookmark89)

[et al., 2023](#_bookmark89)). It raises arginine levels while decreasing citrulline and ornithine levels in the liver and brain ([Zhang et al., 2018](#_bookmark121); [Li et al.,](#_bookmark77) [2020a](#_bookmark77)), causing an imbalance of free amino acids. Also, it reduces fish immunity because of stress, which causes massive deaths and financial loss ([Harper and Wolf, 2009](#_bookmark58)). There are various innovative techniques for effectively removing ammonia levels in aquaculture systems which includes Geo-biofilters ([Varma et al., 2024](#_bookmark112)), Geomaterial Adsorbents ([Belhouchet et al., 2024](#_bookmark30)), Electrocoagulation ([Visconcin et al., 2024](#_bookmark114)), Ultrasonic Vibration ([Fuyu et al., 2023](#_bookmark52)). However, these methods are complex and costly. Thus, it is acknowledged that the use of herbal remedies can effectively lower the ammonia levels in aquaculture ponds and strengthens natural immunity and resistance against infection of fish ([Fayed et al., 2019](#_bookmark51); [Dawood et al., 2021](#_bookmark43)). It is one sustainable and environmentally beneficial method of removing toxins from contami-nated soil and water ([Ram and Parvati, 2012](#_bookmark95)).

MAPs can be utilized as prophylactic and therapeutic measure in the aquaculture industry ([Ahmadifar et al., 2021a](#_bookmark20)). The quantity of flavo-noids, tannins, alkaloids, and other bioactive phytochemicals with antibacterial properties found in medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs) makes them suitable for use in plant-assisted bioremediation in aqua-culture. Supplementation of cornelian cherry fruit extract in fish feed enhanced immune system and growth performance of common carp ([Ahmadifar et al., 2022](#_bookmark22)). However, ginger powder does not promote zebra fish growth, although dietary ginger may have antioxidant effects, since zebrafish showed increased catalase gene expression ([Ahmadifar](#_bookmark19) [et al., 2019](#_bookmark19)). MAPs are also used for their natural antimicrobial prop-erties which effectively combat various pathogens, including protozoan and bacterial infections ([Gadallah et al., 2024](#_bookmark53); [Shohreh et al., 2024](#_bookmark103)). More than thirty plant species have been reported to have potential as treatments for protozoan infections ([Gadallah et al., 2024](#_bookmark53)). [Yousefi et al.](#_bookmark118) [(2019)](#_bookmark118) reported that rosemary leaf powder enhanced growth and im-mune system in _Cyprinus carpio_ fingerlings.

For the present study, two medicinal plants were chosen, namely Indian gooseberry and blond psyllium. The Indian gooseberry is exten-sively distributed across tropical and subtropical regions, including South-east Asia, China, India, and Indonesia. It is classified under the family Euphorbiaceae ([Liu et al., 2008](#_bookmark80)). It is primarily used in processed form because it is intensely acidic and astringent to be consumed raw. This fruit is a highly beneficial plant due to its abundance of nutrients ([Raj et al., 2019](#_bookmark94)). In addition to its therapeutic qualities, this fruit finds extensive application in the culinary and cosmetic sectors ([Kumar et al.,](#_bookmark74) [2012](#_bookmark74)). blond Psyllium belongs to the family Plantaginaceae. It is native to West Asia and the Mediterranean region and is primary used for the production of mucilage. It was brought to India and is cultivated pri-marily in Gujarat and a few areas of Rajasthan. It is also found in Sindh, Baluchistan, and the plains and low hills of Punjab from the Sutlej westward. They are naturally occurring substances that protect both people and animals by regulating immunity and acting as antioxidants, anti-inflammatory agents, and anti-carcinogens ([Ahmadifar et al.,](#_bookmark21) [2021b](#_bookmark21); [Dawood et al., 2021](#_bookmark43); [Meccariello and D’Angelo, 2021](#_bookmark82); [Ojeaburu](#_bookmark87) [and Oriakhi, 2021](#_bookmark87)). Apart from acting as a substrate for periphyton in aquaculture, MAPs, their constituents, or their by-products are effective biosorbents that eliminate pollutants ([Krishnani and Ayyappan, 2006](#_bookmark72)). But their potential to disclose the biological mechanisms defending various fish species against a range of ailments has not yet been fully realized ([Hern´andez-Contreras and Herna´ndez, 2020](#_bookmark60); [Reverter et al.,](#_bookmark97) [2017](#_bookmark97); [Tadese et al., 2022](#_bookmark109)). Within this framework, the study has been conducted to evaluate the controlled release effect of Indian gooseberry (_Phylanthus emblica_) product microencapsulated with hydrogel derived from blond psyllium (_Plantado ovata_) on ammonia elimination in aquaponic water, stress mitigation, and its immunostimulatory effect on growth performance of _Pangasianodon hypophthalmus_ in semi-biofloc system of aquaculture.

# Materials and methods

- 1.  _Preparation of MAPs derived products_

Two MAPs viz. _Plantado ovata_ (blond psyllium), and _Phylanthus emblica_ (Indian gooseberry) were used for the experiments. The MAPs were collected from ICAR- Directorate of Medicinal & Aromatic Plants Research (ICAR-DMAPR), Anand, Gujarat. _P. ovata_ was used as a binder to develop the products due to its adhesive property and nontoxic nature ([Kreitschitz et al. 2021](#_bookmark71)). Blond psyllium seeds and Indian gooseberry fruits were dried in a dryer overnight at 45 ◦C to remove the moisture content. The MAPs were separately blended into a fine powder using an electric blender and passed through a sieve. For product formulation of Indian gooseberry + blond psyllium ball, a 2:1 ratio comprising 40 g of dried and ground Indian gooseberry and 20 g of dried and ground blond psyllium was thoroughly mixed. Then, 80 mL of distilled water was added to the mixture to form a dough, which was then made into small balls and dried at 45 ◦C. For the preparation of blond psyllium ball, 20 g of blond psyllium was mixed with 60 mL of distilled water to form a dough. This dough was then shaped into small balls and dried at 45 ◦C. Following the drying process, the samples were stored in airtight con-tainers until further used for experimentation.

- 1.  _Details of the experiment_

An experiment was conducted following a completely randomized design (CRD) using _Pangasianodon hypophthalmus_ fingerlings as experi-mental fish. To test the decontaminating efficacy of MAPs derived products, fish were exposed to different concentrations of total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) for a duration of 45 days. The study was divided into three groups with triplicates:

1. C (Control): no MAPs added
2. T1: Blond psyllium ball @1 g added after every ammonia spiking
3. T2: Blond psyllium + Indian gooseberry ball added @3 g after every ammonia spiking

Different concentrations of ammonium sulfate were spiked to study the efficiency of MAPs in removing ammonia from the fish cultured water. In the first week, 2 ppm of ammonium sulfate spiked, then gradually increased till the fifth week, i.e., 4 ppm, 6 ppm, 8 ppm, and 10 ppm. The ammonia removal observation was stopped when a treatment reached more than 80 % removal for each spiking.

- 1.  _Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy_

The determination of functional groups in blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry was carried out using Fourier Transform Infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy (ThermoFisher) with the potassium bromide (KBr) pellet technique.

- 1.  _X-ray diffraction (XRD)_

The XRD pattern of Indian gooseberry and brown psyllium was identified at the ICAR-National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning, Nagpur, India. The analysis was carried out through a dif-fracted beam graphite-monochromator and a PANalytical X’Pert-ProXRD diffractometer with Cu radiation (40 kV and 40 mA). With a step size of 0.02 degrees and a count time of 3 s per step, the data collection spanned a 2θ range of 5 to 65 degrees.

- 1.  _Extraction and analysis of plant bioactives using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS)_

LC-MS was used for characterization of blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry at ICAR-National research centres for Grapes, Pune, India.

For extraction of bioactive compounds, 100 mg of plant material was sonicated with 1 mL of methanol.

- 1.  _Water quality attributes_

Throughout the experiments, the parameters pertaining to water quality, such as dissolved oxygen (DO), alkalinity, and hardness, were monitored using the standard protocol ([American Public Health Asso-ciation, 2005](#_bookmark25)). The temperature was measured by a mercury ther-mometer and pH was measured using a pH meter, CyberScan pc 510 (Eutech instrument). TDS was measured by HM Digital TDS tester, and TSS was measured in Imhoff Cone. Total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) and nitrite nitrogen (NO2 -N) were analyzed using the standard method of APHA, 2005, and the absorbance was recorded using a UV/ VIS spec-trophotometer, model 2080 (Analytical Technologies Limited). pH and alkalinity were continuously measured at 12 h intervals after each TAN spike until a reduction of more than 80 % was observed in one of the treatments.

- 1.  _Growth parameters_

Fish were procured from TriShakti Fish Farm, Kurla, and acclimated for a month prior to the experiment at ICAR-CIFE, Mumbai, India. Ten fingerlings, having an average weight of 11.32 ± 0.05 g, were stocked in plastic crates measuring 0.75 × 0.50 × 0.45 m, which were filled with aquaponic water. Fish were fed with Growel feed containing 30 % crude protein twice daily, and feeding was adjusted based on their feeding response throughout the trial. Sampling was carried out intermittently every 15 days during the investigations. The evaluation of different growth parameters was carried out using the following formula ([El-Saidy and Gaber, 2005](#_bookmark49)):

1. SGR (%) = _ln_(_Final weight_)—_ln_(_Initial weight_) × 100

_Number of days_

1. NBG (g) = _Final Total Biomass_ — _Initial Total Biomass_

_Feed given_ (_Dry weight_) _Body weight gain_ (_Wet weight_)

c) FCR =

1. PER (%) = _wet weightgain in fish_ × 100

_Protein fed_

SGR = Specific Growth Rate; NBG = Net Biomass Gain; FCR = Feed Conversion Ratio; PER = Protein Efficiency Ratio.

- 1.  _Blood and serum collection_

Anesthetic procedures were carried out using clove oil prior to blood collection ([Devi and Kamilya, 2019](#_bookmark44)). Blood was collected from the caudal vein with a 2 mL hypodermic syringe and 24-gauge needles. 2.75

% EDTA was used as an anticoagulant for plasma collection ([Linga Prabu](#_bookmark79) [et al., 2022](#_bookmark79)), while no anticoagulant was used for serum. The serum was stored in a sterile vial at —20 ◦C until used for further analysis.

- 1.  _Statistical analysis_

The SPSS 25.0 software (IBM, Chicago, USA) was used to analyze the data using one-way ANOVA in order to determine whether there were any significant differences between the treatment means ([Duncan,](#_bookmark45) [1955](#_bookmark45)). Tukey’s multiple range test was used to identify and assess sig-nificant differences between means. The linear and quadratic effects of inciting factors on the observed response parameters were found using polynomial contrasts. The results are represented as mean ± S.E. A 5 % probability threshold was used to determine the significance level. After verifying the homogeneity and normality of variance, the arcsine transformation was applied to all percentage data.

# Results

- 1.  _Characterization of blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry_
        1. _FT-IR spectra_

The FT-IR spectra of blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry are pre-sented in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark5). The absorption peak of blond psyllium showed at wavenumber 3277.5 cm—1, 2923.9 cm—1, 1634.03 cm—1, 1538.08 cm—1, 1403.6 cm—1 and 1016.91 cm—1. While the spectra of Indian gooseberry were observed at 3280.61 cm—1, 2918.14 cm—1, 1714.63 cm—1, 1608.76

cm—1, 1315.84 cm—1, 1206.38 cm—1, and 1016.51 cm—1.

- -   1.  _X-ray diffraction (XRD)_

An X-ray diffractometer (XRD) is used in the microscopic charac-terization process to analyze the sample’s structure. The XRD spectra of blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry are presented in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark6). The XRD spectrum of Indian gooseberry shows a wide range of peak patterns as an amorphous indicator and a succession of sharp peaks as a crystal indi-cator, while narrow peak patterns are observed in blond psyllium.

- -   1.  _Liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS)_

Liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis and quantification of possible bioactives in blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry are presented in [Figs. 3 and 4](#_bookmark7). Flavonoids and phenolics have been reported in the Indian gooseberry extract. The main flavonoids identified were quercetin, gallic acid, and quinic acid. LC-MS profile of phenolic acid/ flavonoids, essential amino acids and vitamins of Indian gooseberry is presented in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark8). Results of the present study clearly indicated methanolic extract obtained after sonication proved to be effective in enhancing extraction of bioactive compounds from plant materials. [Annegowda et al. (2012)](#_bookmark26) conducted to examine the effects of sonication treatments on phenolics and other antioxidant compounds in starfruits extracted in methanol and water and concluded that meth-anolic extracts obtained after 30 min of sonication proved to be the best treatment, which exhibited significantly higher extractability.

- 1.  _Water quality attributes_

The physicochemical parameters of the experimental waters during the study period are presented in [Table 1](#_bookmark9). The DO, temperature, hard-ness, alkalinity, pH, TDS, and TSS are within the optimal range for catfish culture ([Biswas et al., 2020](#_bookmark31)). Temperature was observed between the range of 27.3 ◦C to 29.3 ◦C. Hardness was in the range of 140 mgL—1 to 188 mgL—1. During the experimental period alkalinity was observed within the range of 80 mgL—1 to 204 mgL—1 and pH was observed be-tween 6.39 and 8.04. The alkalinity and pH of the water were greatly affected particularly at the later stage of the experiment. pH dropped below 7 after the spiking of 8 ppm TAN, hence, liming was done to raise the pH to about 7.5 in all the tanks. The reduction in pH with the reduction of 10 ppm TAN concentrations among the treatments is pre-sented in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark10). [Fig. 6](#_bookmark11) shows the pH level after the reduction of different concentrations of TAN in the treatments, and the increase in pH after liming. Alkalinity was higher in the control group as compared to the treatment groups due to lower nitrification rate and ammonia removal in control. Continuous aeration was provided in all the tanks to maintain DO concentration above 5 mgL—1. TSS were higher in the T2 group i.e.

12.8 mgL—1 to 13.5 mgL—1 compare to T1 and control.

- 1.  _TAN removal and nitrite_

At the initial spiking of 2 ppm, T2 significantly removed 88.77 ±

1.03 % followed by T1 (57.34 ± 4.45 %) and control (21.11 ± 3.73 %.) in 24 h. The same trend was followed till 3rd week, but the duration was varied depending on the concentrations. It takes 48 h. and 60 h. for 4 ppm and 6 ppm respectively. Even though the ammonia increased, the efficiency of ammonia removal also gradually increased as the

experiment progressed. In the 4th week, ammonia removal was faster even if the concentration was higher, i.e. 8 ppm. In the fifth week, i.e., 10 ppm spiking, there was less ammonia reduction, which is correlated with the drop in pH levels ([Abdel-Tawwab et al., 2020](#_bookmark16)) due to the nitrification process. At 84 h., T2 significantly removed 94.10 ± 0.32 % of TAN, while TAN removal of the control group showed only 1.43 ± 9.09

- 1.  _Fish growth_

In the present study, T2 showed significantly highest final total biomass (FTB) (221.48 ± 1.28 g), NBG (107.69 ± 0.90 g), and SGR

(1.48 ± 0.01 %/day). Additionally, low FCR (1.75 ± 0.03) and high PER (1.91 ± 0.04) were also observed in T2. In contrary, control showed lowest (_p_ < 0.05) FTB (169.88 ± 0.94 g), NBG (55.31 ± 1.52) and SGR

(0.88 ± 0.03 %). The slow reduction of ammonia led to fish stress and

poor growth performance in the control group, as evident by inferior performances in growth indices and the high FCR (2.22 ± 0.13) and low PER (1.50 ± 0.08) in the control group. Throughout the entire experi-ment, there was no mortality reported. The growth performance and feed efficiency of _P. hypophthalmus_ are presented in [Table 4](#_bookmark14).

# Discussion

Blond psyllium showed a broad peak at 3277.5 cm—1 which can be attributed to the –OH stretching band. The peak at 2923.9 cm—1 was due to the C–H stretching of cellulose. The band at 1634.03 cm—1 was due to the C–C stretching band, and 1538.08 cm—1 was due to the N–O stretching band ([Singh et al., 2023](#_bookmark105)). The stretching of the carboxyl group (—COO—) of uronic acids is responsible for the band at 1403.6 cm—1 ([Timilsena et al., 2016](#_bookmark110)). The absorption peak at 3280.61 cm—1 was observed in Indian gooseberry, which was due to –OH stretching vi-bration. The band at 2918.14 cm—1 was due to the presence of alkane C–H stretching. The band at 1714.63 was due to the C–H bending of aromatic compounds. The band at 1608.76 cm—1 was due to the C–C stretching of the alkene group ([Gupta et al., 2021](#_bookmark57)). The band at 1315.84 cm—1 was due to the O–H bending of phenol, and the 1206.38 cm—1 band was due to the C–O stretching of alkyl aryl ether. The strong band at 1016.91 cm—1 and 1016.51 cm—1 of blond psyllium and Indian gooseberry, respectively, was due to the polysaccharide (1–4)-glycosidic linkage and their corresponding monosaccharides ([Nikonenko et al.,](#_bookmark86) [2000](#_bookmark86)).

The X-ray diffractometer investigation revealed that Indian goose-berry has a crystalline-amorphous microstructure. [Caparino et al.](#_bookmark37) [(2012)](#_bookmark37) have noticed a similar pattern in the experimental outcome. Furthermore, the XRD spectra of Indian gooseberry powder and those of other vitamin C-containing fruits, including mango ([Caparino et al.,](#_bookmark37) [2012](#_bookmark37)), jamun pulp powder, papaya, sapota, and guava ([Athmaselvi](#_bookmark27) [et al., 2014](#_bookmark27)), are nearly comparable. The Indian gooseberry fruit’s unique diffraction peak of amorphous structures is located at 19◦. It is exclusive to Indian gooseberry fruit it does not exist in other fruits that contain vitamin C.

Isabgol is a hydrophilic material in nature and is well known for its water uptake properties, gelling capabilities, soluble and insoluble fibre contents and surface structure, due to the presence of natural poly-saccharides and contains high percentage of hemicelluloses. It is not 100 % water soluble polysaccharide, which has similar molecular con-stituents has more or less similar physiological functions to other naturally sourced polysaccharides like alginate, and guar gum. 1-O-(3,4,5-Trimethoxybenzoyl)-beta-L-galactopyranose (_m_/_z_ 397.1), 2-(3,4-Dihydroxyphenyl)-5,7-dihydroxy-4-oxo-4H-chromen-3-yl 6-O-β-D-

xylopyranosyl-β-D-glucopyranoside (m/z 597.1), and 2-(3,4-Dihydrox-yphenyl)ethyl 3-O-(6-deoxy-β-L-mannopyranosyl)-6-O-\[(2E)-3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)-2-propenoyl\]-β-D-glucopyranoside (m/z 625.2), 5,7-dihydroxy-2-(4-hydroxy-3-{\[(2_S_,3_R_,4_S_,5_S_,6_R_)-3,4,5-trihydroxy-6-(hydroxymethyl)oxan-2-yl\]oxy}phenyl)-3-methoxy-4H-chromen-4-one

(m/z 479.11), 5,7-Dihydroxy-2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-6,8-bis\[3,4,5-trihy-droxy-6-(hydroxymethyl) tetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-yl\]-4H-chromen-4-one (m/z 595.1), 4-Indolecarbaldehyde (m/z 146), Kaempferol (m/z 287), apigenin (m/z 271) were found to be prominent polysaccharides, metabolites, fatty acids, amino acids, phenolics, flavonoids, and

![](data:image/png;base64,)

**Fig. 3.** LC-MS spectra of (A) Blond psyllium and (B) Indian gooseberry.

antioxidants in isabgol. The metabolites apigenin and kaempferol have also been detected. Psyllium contains phenolics, flavonoids, terpenoids, tryptophan and iridoid glycosides ([Samuelsen, 2000](#_bookmark100)). [Patel et al. (2020)](#_bookmark90) demonstrated metabolomics in developing psyllium fruit, which is a rich source of primary metabolites (ω-3 and ω-6 fatty acids and amino-acids), secondary metabolites and natural antioxidants.

As the culture period advanced, higher TDS and TSS were observed in the treatment tanks where the organic MAP products are added, as compared to the control group. This is due to the accumulation of organic and inorganic substances in the treatment tanks as it is a zero-water exchange system ([Rafiee and Saad, 2005](#_bookmark93)). The temperature throughout the experiment falls within the optimal range for tropical aquaculture ([Boyd and Tucker, 2014](#_bookmark33)).

The reduction in alkalinity and pH of the water particularly at the later stage of the experiment was due to the native aquaponics hetero-trophic and/or autotrophic bacteria consuming alkalinity for metabo-lizing and/or nitrifying the TAN spiked in the system ([Ebeling et al.,](#_bookmark47) [2006](#_bookmark47); [Boyd et al., 2016](#_bookmark34); [Martínez-Alvarez et al., 2018](#_bookmark81); [Bozorg-Haddad](#_bookmark35) [et al., 2021](#_bookmark35)). As a result, liming was carried out using CaCO3 to bring the pH to about 7.5 in all the experimental tanks as it was reduced below 7 after the spiking of 8 ppm TAN. CaCO3 was used to stabilize the pH ([Boyd and Tucker, 2014](#_bookmark33); [Somridhivej and Boyd, 2017](#_bookmark106)). pH was

maintained above 7 during the initial phase of the experiment since alkalinity was within the ideal range. As a result of the buffering ca-pacity being lost when the alkalinity level dropped below 100 mgL—1, pH decreased below 7.

When the ammonia concentration is higher, it takes a longer time to remove ammonia from water. In the 4th week, the efficiency of ammonia removal was faster as the experiment progressed. This is due to the blond psyllium microspheres that might be used to control the release of Indian gooseberry products and produce carriers for pro-longed drug release. Such natural polymers are utilized as drug carriers since they are non-toxic, easy to obtain, biodegradable, and biocom-patible. Several natural polysaccharides have been studied in relation to hydrogel synthesis for medication delivery systems ([Wolinsky et al.,](#_bookmark117) [2012](#_bookmark117); [Kratz et al., 2013](#_bookmark70)). Hydrogels are beneficial for a wide range of biomedical applications because of their remarkable water retention capacity, which is fairly close to that of natural living tissues. The isabgol seed has been reported to contain 89 % carbohydrate ([Jose and](#_bookmark65) [Kumar, 2022](#_bookmark65)) which makes it an excellent source of carbon for the heterotrophic bacteria in the system that will aid in ammonia utilization and/or conversion. As a result, faster ammonia removal is observed in T1 and T2 in comparison to the control. Various fabrication strategies have been used to adapt these hydrogel systems in microsphere

In recent decades, several studies have focused on investigating the medicinal plant’s potential benefits, with promising outcomes including the decrease in ammonia levels associated with aquaculture through the use of various extracts ([Santacruz-Reyes and Chien, 2012](#_bookmark101); [Castillo et al.,](#_bookmark38) [2015](#_bookmark38)). It has been proved that some medicinal plant-based products such as mint, _aloe vera_, banana stem ([Kate et al., 2023](#_bookmark67)), and yucca extract ([Castillo et al., 2015](#_bookmark38); [Adegbeye et al., 2019](#_bookmark17)) are a crucial strategy for successfully minimizing the negative consequences of increased ammonia levels in aquaculture. Additionally, [Krishnani et al. (2002)](#_bookmark73) investigated the extent to which neem (_Azadirachta indica_) oil and powder removed TAN from coastal shrimp aquaculture water. The hy-droxyl and the carboxyl group present in the isabgol and Indian gooseberry as shown in the FTIR analyses has been reported to be the primary group responsible for ammonium adsorption ([Wahab et al.,](#_bookmark115) [2010](#_bookmark115)). This also contributes to the ammonia reduction in the treatment tanks. The current research revealed that Indian gooseberry is efficient in the removal of ammonia, which aligns with the hypothesis of

As the current study is based on a semi-biofloc system, it lowers aquaculture pollution, boosts productivity, improves feed conversion ratio, and produces nutrient-dense food ([Bossier and](#_bookmark32) [Ekasari, 2017](#_bookmark32); [Khanjani and Sharifinia, 2020](#_bookmark68)). According to [Van Doan](#_bookmark111) [et al. (2022)](#_bookmark111), Indian gooseberry fruit extract promotes the growth of Nile tilapia (_Oreochromis niloticus_) cultured in a biofloc system, which lends credence to the current findings in _Pangasianodon hypophthalmus_ growth. It has been shown that Indian gooseberry is a valuable plant with a variety of biological activity ([Jantan et al., 2019](#_bookmark64)) and nutritional value. It contains a number of beneficial components, including phenolic compounds, vitamin C, and iron (III) ([Irsyam et al., 2020](#_bookmark63)). Emblicanin A, emblicanin B, gallic acid, tannins, ellagitannins, and polyphenols are some of its main constituents ([Ahmad et al., 2021](#_bookmark18); [Chauhan et al., 2021](#_bookmark39); [Li et al., 2020b](#_bookmark78)). Calcium, lysine, methionine, nicotinic acid, phosphorus, riboflavin, and tryptophane are abundant in Indian gooseberry fruit. These compounds stimulate the excretion of digestive enzymes, which improves feed utilization and consequently promotes fish growth ([Omitoyin et al., 2019](#_bookmark88)). Indian gooseberry is also well known for its immunoregulatory properties against a variety of

Studies on terrestrial animals have shown that its bioactive components enhance their immune response and resilience to disease ([Rizwan et al., 2021](#_bookmark98); [Sharma et al., 2021](#_bookmark102)). At 10 ppm of ammonia, fish performance is slightly impacted, but the immunological and antioxidative responses are substantially compro-mised by high levels of ammonia toxicity ([Qi et al., 2017](#_bookmark92)).

Ammonia toxicity in aquatic animals can compromise immune function and exacerbate inflammation ([Cheng et al., 2015](#_bookmark41)). Aquatic

animals’ health and performance are negatively impacted by water-borne ammonia, which is a serious hazard ([Yue et al., 2010](#_bookmark120); [Cheng et al.,](#_bookmark41) [2015](#_bookmark41); [Qi et al., 2017](#_bookmark92)). Blood biochemical and immunological indices are thought to be helpful methods for producing reliable information on the wellbeing state of the fish ([Singh et al., 2019](#_bookmark104)). Fish have a number of defense mechanisms, including antioxidant and physical defenses, as well as mechanisms for prevention and repair. Enzymatic antioxidants include glutathione peroxidase (GPx), catalase (CAT), and superoxide

contribute to ammonia decontamination, alleviating stress, and growth of _Pangasianodon hypophthalmus_. Indian gooseberry fruit micro-encapsulated with blond psyllium successfully minimizes the effect of ammonia toxicity in aquaculture. However, when the pH and alkalinity of the water drop below 7 and 100 mgL—1, respectively, buffering ca-pacity is lost, and the rate of ammonia reduction slows down. Hydrogel from blond psyllium holds the capacity of MAPs to remove ammonia from water and slowly release it. This will be beneficial to system maintenance over an extended duration. As the culture proceeded, the accumulation of ammonia also increased; therefore, this product will help to alleviate the stress caused by ammonia in biofloc or zero water systems. It’s interesting to note that a higher rate of ammonia elimina-tion and less stress contributed to improved fish growth. Application of medicinal and aromatic plant coupled with hydrogel-based plant prod-uct is conceptualised as a novel and environmentally viable approach for application of environmental and health management of aquaculture.

observed in the control group (6.66 ± 0.12 mg/mL) are indicative of stress due to longer exposure to ammonia, as it is known to drop in response to many environmental stressors ([Akhtar et al., 2013](#_bookmark23) & [Kumar](#_bookmark75) [et al., 2017](#_bookmark75)). High concentrations of immune-related total serum pro-tein, such as albumin and globulin, which comprise the major protein groups, are also associated with active innate immunity ([Rao et al.,](#_bookmark96)

[2006](#_bookmark96)). Total serum protein (_P_ < 0.05) and globulin (_P_ \> 0.05) levels

were observed to be higher in T2, highlighting the possibility of mi-crobial flocs acting as an immune-stimulant. According to reports from many species, an increase in the plasma glucose level in fish exposed to ammonia implies stress ([Barbieri and Bondioli, 2015](#_bookmark29)). When fish are under stress, cortisol influences the process of gluconeogenesis, which produces glucose from noncarbohydrate sources ([Vijayan et al., 1997](#_bookmark113)). In our investigation, the control group’s glucose level was shown to be significantly higher, while T2 showed a significantly lower glucose level. The presence of bioactive compounds in isabgol and Indian gooseberry are evident as illustrated by the LC-MS analyses in the study. Bioactive compounds have been reported to be passively released during the decomposition of plants ([Huang et al., 2020](#_bookmark61)). According to [Elbialy et al.](#_bookmark48) [(2021)](#_bookmark48), supplementing water with _Yucca schidigera_ extract alleviated the adverse effect of ammonia poisoning in nile tilapia, attributed to its anti-inflammatory properties, strong antioxidant activity, and free radical scavenging capability. This may explain the improved performance observed in fish from treatment groups relative to the control group. T2 performed noticeably better than T1 and control in the hematological and serum biochemical parameters of _P. hypophthalmus._ This suggests the amla incorporated in the isabgol was effective in alleviating stress and improving overall health, resulting in better growth performance as compared to isabgol alone and control. The dual benefits of isabgol + amla balls (environmental improvement by lowering TAN concentration from water and antioxidant supplements) to maximize fish health and growth performance highlight the significance of stress management.
